q: A customer wants evidence that a SaaS provider's security controls were not only well designed but also effective over the last 12 months. Which report is MOST appropriate?
explain: SOC 2 Type II covers the Trust Services Criteria (including Security) and tests operating effectiveness over a period. Type I is design at a point in time, SOC 3 is a summary without test details, and SOC 1 relates to financial reporting.

q: A provider publishes a report on its website as marketing evidence of security, without an NDA. Which report is this MOST LIKELY?
explain: SOC 3 is for general use. SOC 1, SOC 2, and ISAE 3402 are restricted-use reports distributed to users and their auditors, usually under NDA.

q: The financial auditor of an EU company needs assurance about a cloud provider's controls that affect the company's financial statements. Which international standard is MOST relevant?
explain: ISAE 3402 is the international equivalent of SOC 1 (SSAE 18 AT-C 320) and focuses on controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting. ISO 27001 is ISMS certification, and 27036 covers supplier relationships.

q: A company uses a provider's new AI service in a region in Asia. The provider's SOC 2 Type II covers IaaS services in the EU and the US for a period that ended before that service was launched. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: The report covers all services because it was issued for the provider as an organization.
The report provides no assurance for the AI service or the Asian region; other evidence or the next report should be requested.
The report is invalid and the provider should be rejected.
It is enough to request a bridge letter for the existing scope.
explain: The scope statement limits assurance to the listed services, locations, and period. A bridge letter covers the time gap for the same scope, not new services. The report is not invalid; it simply does not cover that service.

q: A provider's SOC 2 report lists a number of complementary user entity controls (CUECs). What does this mean for the customer?
options: They are controls the provider plans to introduce next year.
They are controls of the provider's subservice organizations excluded by the carve-out method.
They are controls the customer must implement itself for the provider's controls to be effective.
They are optional recommendations with no effect on the auditor's opinion.
explain: CUECs are the auditor's assumptions about controls on the customer's side (e.g., user account management, MFA). If the customer does not implement them, the assurance from the report does not fully apply to it.

q: An organization is preparing for the first ISO/IEC 27001 certification of its cloud environment. What is the BEST first step?
options: A gap analysis of the current state against the requirements of the standard.
explain: A gap analysis shows what is missing (clauses 4 to 10 and the Annex A controls) and provides a plan. A tool or a single policy are parts of the solution, and an audit without preparation leads to nonconformities.

q: Business process owners assess the risks and effectiveness of controls in their own cloud applications through workshops. What is this technique called and what is its main weakness?
options: Baseline comparison; it does not take risk into account.
Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA); lower objectivity because they assess themselves.
explain: RCSA involves the first line and is cheap, but the assessment is subjective. That is why it is supplemented with independent checks (the second and third lines, external audit).

q: A US electric utility is considering storing BES Cyber System Information in the public cloud. Which regulatory framework is MOST directly applicable?
explain: NERC CIP protects the bulk electric system in North America, including protection of BCSI. HITECH is healthcare, PCI DSS cards, FERPA education.

q: An internal auditor needs to plan an audit of IAM controls in a multi-cloud environment. What should be done AFTER defining the audit objectives?
options: Define the scope: systems, providers, locations, period, and what the providers' reports cover.
Immediately issue findings based on last year's report.
Request physical access to all providers' data centers.
explain: Planning goes from objectives to scope, then execution and reporting. In the cloud, the scope must take into account what is covered by the CSP's reports and what is the customer's responsibility.

q: Which data role has ultimate accountability for data classification and for deciding who may access the data?
explain: The data owner is a business role with ultimate accountability. The custodian implements technical protection, the steward takes care of quality and meaning, and the processor processes on behalf of the controller.

q: An IT operations team performs backup, encryption, and assignment of data access according to the business owner's instructions. What role does the team have?
explain: The custodian stores and technically protects the data day to day according to the owner's requirements, but does not decide on classification or the purpose of processing.

q: A company buys cyber insurance to cover the costs of a possible data breach in the cloud. Which risk treatment strategy is this and what remains with the company?
options: Transfer; accountability, legal obligations, and reputational risk remain with the company.
Mitigate; the likelihood of a breach is reduced.
explain: Insurance transfers the financial consequences, but the controller remains accountable to the regulator and data subjects, and reputation cannot be transferred. Insurance does not reduce the likelihood of the event.

q: A bank with a low risk appetite is assessing a provider that frequently introduces new services in preview and has an aggressive approach to innovation. What is MOST important to assess?
options: The compatibility of the provider's risk appetite and risk profile with the bank's appetite, along with controls and policies that bridge the gap.
Only the price of the services.
The number of the provider's regions.
Whether the provider has a mobile management app.
explain: Assessing the provider's risk management program includes controls, methodologies, policies, risk profile, and appetite. A mismatched appetite means the bank must restrict usage (e.g., prohibiting preview services by policy) or choose another provider.

q: A system worth EUR 400,000 has an exposure factor of 25% for a certain scenario, and the scenario is expected once every four years. What is the ALE?
explain: SLE = 400,000 × 0.25 = EUR 100,000. ARO = 0.25. ALE = SLE × ARO = EUR 25,000. A control that costs more than the reduction in ALE is not economically justified.

q: The CISO wants to show management an early warning of rising cloud configuration risk. Which metric is MOST appropriate?
options: The total number of logs received in the SIEM.
A KRI: the number of critical misconfigurations (e.g., publicly exposed storage) and their trend relative to a threshold.
explain: A Key Risk Indicator measures exposure and warns before an incident, especially when the trend is shown relative to the tolerance threshold. The other options do not measure risk.

q: A US public company uses a SaaS ERP for financial reporting. Which regulatory transparency requirement MOST directly brings those cloud controls into scope?
options: SOX Section 404 (internal control over financial reporting)
explain: SOX 404 requires an assessment of ICFR, so systems that affect financial statements, including a SaaS ERP, are in scope; evidence of the provider's controls is usually a SOC 1 report.

q: A company has an umbrella contract with a consulting firm and, for each new migration project, signs a separate document with deliverables, deadlines, and price. What is that separate document called?
explain: A Statement of Work defines a specific job under the umbrella Master Service Agreement. An SLA defines a measurable service level, and an OLA is an internal agreement between teams.

q: When negotiating with a cloud provider, which clause BEST protects the customer from the risk of losing data upon contract termination?
options: A clause on returning data in an agreed, usable format and timeframe, transition assistance, and confirmed deletion after the return.
A clause on service credits for availability below 99.9%.
A clause on the competent court.
A clause on automatic contract renewal.
explain: Termination clauses with data return, transition, and deletion directly address exit risk and lock-in. Service credits and the competent court do not guarantee access to data.

q: A company depends on specialized software from a small vendor whose financial situation is uncertain. Which measure BEST mitigates the risk of the vendor going out of business?
options: A longer contract with the vendor.
An escrow arrangement for source code, data, and documentation with clear release triggers.
explain: The escrow agent releases the source code and other materials upon defined events (bankruptcy, end of support). A longer contract, an SLA, and an audit don't help if the vendor ceases to exist.

q: A large public cloud provider refuses to allow a customer a physical audit of its data centers. What is the BEST approach for a customer that is not in a specially regulated sector?
options: Secure by contract the regular delivery of independent reports (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, CSA STAR) and incident information, and review them regularly.
Test the provider's infrastructure without permission.
Accept the service without any assurance.
explain: With large CSPs, the right to audit is most often exercised through third-party reports, because physical audits by thousands of customers are not feasible and would endanger other tenants. Regulated sectors (e.g., under DORA) may have stronger access rights.

q: Which part of ISO/IEC 27036 provides guidelines for the security of relationships with cloud service suppliers?
explain: 27036-4 is dedicated to the security of cloud services. Part 1 is the overview and concepts, part 2 requirements, part 3 the hardware, software, and services supply chain.

q: A company's SaaS vendor runs on the infrastructure of another public cloud provider. How does the company BEST manage this fourth-party risk?
options: Ignore it, because the company has no contract with the fourth party.
Contract directly for the service with the IaaS provider.
Require the SaaS vendor to move to its own data center.

Require by contract a subprocessor list, flow-down of security requirements, and notification of changes, and review reports covering subservice organizations (inclusive, or a separate report in case of carve-out).
explain: Supply chain management requires visibility into subcontractors and passing obligations through contracts. The company has no direct contract with the fourth party, but the risk exists and is managed through the vendor.

q: Match the example with the risk treatment strategy.
options: A decision not to move health records to the public cloud.
Introducing encryption with customer keys and a multi-region architecture.
The risk owner formally signs off on accepting the residual risk of a brief outage of the internal wiki.
explain: Not moving the data is avoidance, controls are mitigation, insurance is transfer of financial consequences, and a formally signed-off residual risk is acceptance.

q: Order the steps of planning and conducting an audit of a cloud environment, from first to last.
options: Conduct the audit: collect evidence, interviews, and automated evidence from cloud APIs
Report the findings and follow up on corrective actions, including lessons learned
Define the scope, including providers, locations, period, and coverage by the CSP's reports
explain: An audit starts with objectives, then scope, followed by execution, and finally reporting and follow-up, with lessons learned feeding into the next plan.

q: A hospital is negotiating a contract with a SaaS provider for electronic health records. Mark the clauses that pose the greatest contractual risk to the hospital.
snippet:
Article 7. Customer data
7.1 The Customer retains ownership of all data it enters into the Service.
7.2 The Provider may use customer data, metadata and logs to train its own AI models.
7.3 Data is processed and stored exclusively in EU regions (Frankfurt, Dublin).
Article 12. Termination
12.1 Either party may terminate the agreement with 90 days' notice.
12.2 Upon termination the Provider permanently deletes all customer data within 24 hours, with no export.
12.3 The Provider delivers a written confirmation of data deletion.
Article 15. Assurance
15.1 The Provider delivers a SOC 2 Type II report once a year and a bridge letter when needed.
explain: Line 3 (7.2): the provider gets the right to use patient data, metadata and logs to train its own AI models, which is processing for another purpose and violates data ownership and GDPR; the data ownership clause should explicitly forbid such use, including derived data. Line 7 (12.2): deletion within 24 hours with no export means losing access to the data at termination and vendor lock-in; the contract must guarantee return of data in a usable format within an agreed period and transition assistance, and only then confirmed deletion (12.3). EU location, the notice period and an annual SOC 2 Type II are reasonable clauses.
